headline: Target practice and a tan at Tranquility
summary: Summering at the family's Oyster Bay house, Roosevelt tests a new rifle and scores 67 of 100, calling himself a poor marksman. Rowing has bronzed his upper body, his horse has gone slightly lame, and the swimming is a delight.

events.detail: Tries out a new rifle, scoring 67 out of 100
Notes that steady rowing has deeply tanned him
His horse comes up a little lame
Enjoys sea bathing

tr_quotes.text: Tried the new rifle and made 67 out of 100; it works very well, but I am an awful shot.
The bathing is perfectly delicious.

headline: Rifle practice, then a farewell visit in town
summary: Roosevelt improves to 71 of 100 at the rifle, then heads into New York City to see Annie Murray, who leaves for Europe the next day, and spends a pleasant evening calling on her.

events.detail: Rifle practice, scoring 71 of 100
Goes into the city in the afternoon
Evening visit to Annie Murray before her voyage to Europe

tr_quotes.text: Tried the rifle; 71 out of 100.

headline: Seeing Annie off, then a night sail
summary: At seven in the morning Roosevelt boards the steamer Russia to bid Annie Murray goodbye, finding her pretty but a touch cross. He accompanies Aunt Susie on the trip to Oyster Bay, and that night he and his brother Elliott sail Elliott's 21-foot Daphne across to Rye Harbor, dropping anchor at 1:30 a.m.

events.detail: Says goodbye to Annie Murray aboard the steamer Russia
Escorts Aunt Susie to the family's summer place
Night sail with Elliott on the Daphne, anchoring at Rye Harbor

tr_quotes.text: whom I found very sweet and pretty and a little wee bit out of temper.

headline: Fourth of July sail home from Rye
summary: Roosevelt and Elliott pass the morning and have dinner at the Bulkleys' near Rye, then set off for home at 4:15 p.m., not reaching their Oyster Bay mooring until eleven. The long sail calls up memories of the brothers' many earlier cruises together.

events.detail: Morning and dinner with the Bulkley family
Sails back to Oyster Bay, arriving at 11 p.m.

tr_quotes.text: Enjoyed the sail most thoroughly.

uncertain: Entry lacks the [D] marker but reads as diary; 'Chuff' is a nickname for Elliott.

headline: A tender talk with his mother
summary: Roosevelt and his mother Mittie talk at length, sweetly and sadly, about his late father. Uncle Jimmie Gracie stays over from the city, and he and Roosevelt spend time sailing and rowing.

events.detail: Long talk with his mother about his father's death
Sails and rows with Uncle Jimmie Gracie

headline: Timed row around Centre Island
summary: Roosevelt rows eight miles around Centre Island, logging each landmark against the clock, though low tide forces a half-mile detour and the portage eats 14 minutes. In the afternoon he outshoots Alfred at the rifle, 54 to 18.

events.detail: Rows eight miles around Centre Island, timing himself at each point
Rifle match with Alfred, winning 54 to 18

tr_quotes.text: The portage took 14 minutes, and the tide was so low I had to make a circuit of half a mile.

uncertain: Alfred is presumably cousin Alfred Roosevelt.

headline: Missing Father at Sunday prayers
summary: Roosevelt writes that he is heartsick for his father. At evening singing the family cannot get through a hymn they last sang together on the Sunday he died, and Roosevelt reads Isaiah 55, one of his father's favorites, at prayers.

events.detail: Reads Isaiah 55 aloud at family prayers
Family breaks off a hymn tied to his father's last Sunday

tr_quotes.text: I can never thank God sufficiently for having given me such a lovely, affectionate family.

headline: Winning a rifle match on Mittie's birthday
summary: On his mother's 43rd birthday, Roosevelt wins a shooting match against his cousins West and Emlen, 57 to their 48 and 49. His horse has nearly recovered from its lameness.

events.detail: His mother Mittie turns 43
Wins a rifle match over West and Emlen

tr_quotes.text: My horse now goes very well and is almost entirely free from lameness.

headline: Five months without his father
summary: Marking five months since his father's death, Roosevelt reflects that he feels much older and must now solve his own problems instead of bringing them to his father, whose words and gestures he still recalls with startling clarity.

events.detail: Reflects in his diary on five months since his father died

tr_quotes.text: now I must rely on myself in difficulties, while before I had always carried everything to him.

headline: Stuck in the mud at Lloyd Neck
summary: Rowing around Lloyd Neck, Roosevelt bogs down in the mud flats while carrying his boat across the isthmus and struggles to free himself. On the way home a thunder squall catches him in a stiff southwest wind. Fifteen miles, two plover and two gulls.

events.detail: Rows 15 miles around Lloyd Neck, portaging the isthmus
Shoots two plover and two gulls

tr_quotes.text: got stuck in the mud flats and had hideous work getting out.

headline: Sailing with cousins, doubting himself
summary: Roosevelt sails with West and Alfred, picnic lunch aboard, and splits the rest of the day between riding and rowing. In his diary he frets that so remarkable a father deserved a worthier son.

events.detail: Sailing outing with West and Alfred, lunch aboard
Rides his horse and rows

tr_quotes.text: often feel badly that such a wonderful man as Father should have had a son of so little worth as I am.

headline: Rained in, sizing up his friends
summary: Rain keeps Roosevelt indoors for the first time all summer. He takes stock of his five closest friends: Elliott and Jack Elliott think too well of him, West and Emlen too little, and Alfred judges him about right.

events.detail: Stays indoors all day because of rain
Weighs in his diary how his closest friends regard him

tr_quotes.text: while Alfred takes me for about what I am worth,

uncertain: A word is cut off in the record, apparently 'overestimate'. 'Chuff' is Elliott.

headline: A daily run through the woods
summary: Roosevelt runs a mile flat out through the woods and plans to make it a daily habit.

events.detail: Runs a mile at full speed through the woods

tr_quotes.text: Ran a mile through the woods at speed; shall probably repeat this every day

headline: Pascal and doubts at Communion Sunday
summary: On Communion Sunday Roosevelt copies out a line from Pascal warning against both excluding and relying only on reason, and writes that he finds materialism and superstition equally distasteful. During church he broods on feeling less useful than his father, yet ends on a note of faith.

events.detail: Attends Communion Sunday service
Reads Pascal's apology for religion

tr_quotes.text: Materialism and superstition are equally repugnant to me.
But 'Trust in the Lord and do good!'

uncertain: The Pascal quotation is in French and hard to read in the record, so it is not reproduced.

headline: Hot row and a long gallop
summary: In dead calm and fierce heat at high tide, Roosevelt rows around Centre Island again, the portage this time taking only five minutes. Later he and Emlen gallop out beyond Wheatley and around it.

events.detail: Rows around Centre Island at high tide
Long horseback gallop with Emlen around Wheatley

tr_quotes.text: hotter than tophette

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Riding to Lake Ronkonkoma
summary: Roosevelt and West ride out on a cool, cloudy morning, reach Smithtown by 10:45, push on to Lake Ronkonkoma for supper, and return to Smithtown to sleep. About 35 miles, and his horse finishes as fresh as it began.

events.detail: Rides with West from Oyster Bay to Smithtown
Afternoon ride on to Lake Ronkonkoma for supper
Returns to Smithtown for the night

tr_quotes.text: In all about 35 miles and the horse as fresh as when he started.

headline: Back from Smithtown in the heat
summary: Roosevelt rides home from Smithtown to Oyster Bay in two and a half hours on a very hot day.

events.detail: Rides from Smithtown back to Oyster Bay

tr_quotes.text: Very hot.

uncertain: The diary says 'we' but does not name his companion; presumably West.

headline: Twenty-five miles by oar to Rye
summary: Leaving at 5:15 a.m., Roosevelt rows across to Rye Beach by way of Rocky Point and Oak Bluff, then rows home that evening, a round trip of more than 25 miles in calm, heavy heat. He spots a stormy petrel.

events.detail: Rows from Oyster Bay to Rye Beach and back, over 25 miles
Sees a stormy petrel

tr_quotes.text: In all I rowed rather over 25 miles.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: A one-line Sunday prayer
summary: Roosevelt's diary for this Sunday holds a single line of scripture, a plea from the Gospel of Mark.

events.detail: Records a Biblical prayer in his diary

tr_quotes.text: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief!

headline: Woodcock in the woods
summary: Roosevelt hikes far through woods and fields with his shotgun and brings back four woodcock and two doves.

events.detail: Long hunting walk, bagging four woodcock and two doves

uncertain: The bag tally is unclear in the record; it is read as 4 woodcock.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Visiting the sick, then the Dickeys
summary: In New York City Roosevelt calls on his ailing friend Cassin, then spends the evening with the Dickey family, whose warmth he loves. Young Charles Dickey will enter Harvard next year, and Roosevelt promises himself to help him.

events.detail: Goes into New York City
Visits Cassin, who is ill
Evening with the Dickey family

tr_quotes.text: I like them ever so much, they are so sweet and homelike.

uncertain: Location of the Dickeys' home is not stated beyond 'out here'.

headline: Home again to Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt heads back out to Oyster Bay from his stay near the city.

events.detail: Returns to Oyster Bay

tr_quotes.text: Returned to Oyster Bay.

headline: Rigging a sail on his skiff
summary: Roosevelt fits his small outrigger skiff with a leg-of-mutton sail on a seven-foot mast and takes her out. She points poorly into the wind but holds steady and moves briskly downwind.

events.detail: Rigs a sail on his lapstreak skiff and takes her out

tr_quotes.text: She beats very badly, but is stiff and sails pretty fast off the wind.

uncertain: The record's 'rail' is presumably 'sail'.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Marsh shooting on Alice Lee's birthday
summary: On the day Alice Lee, his future wife, turns 17, Roosevelt rows to Lloyd Neck and paddles the winding marsh channels at high tide, taking shots at herons and snipe. A southerly breeze lets him sail several miles out into the Sound. Elliott leaves on a three-week holiday.

events.detail: Rows to Lloyd Neck and shoots through the marsh, getting three sand snipe
Sails three or four miles into Long Island Sound
Elliott departs for a three-week holiday
Alice Lee turns 17

tr_quotes.text: At high tide it is good fun to paddle through the lagoons and among the winding channels, with an occasional shot at a heron or snipe.

uncertain: 'Chuf fF [Ellie]' read as Elliott.

headline: Rainy woods, then a fine ride
summary: Despite rain, Roosevelt roams the woods with his gun in the morning, bagging a dove and a wild pigeon, and enjoys a splendid ride in the afternoon.

events.detail: Morning walk with his gun; one dove and one wild pigeon
Afternoon horseback ride

headline: Quick row around Centre Island
summary: Roosevelt borrows Alfred's boat and circles Centre Island in an hour and 24 minutes.

events.detail: Rows around Centre Island in 1 hour 24 minutes

tr_quotes.text: Rowed round Centre Island in Alfred's boat in 1h 24m.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Timed circuit of Lloyd Neck
summary: Starting at ten, Roosevelt rows around Lloyd Neck past the Huntington Harbor lighthouse and is home by 1:45. A dead-high tide trims the portage to four minutes.

events.detail: Rows around Lloyd Neck, passing Huntington Harbor lighthouse

tr_quotes.text: Portage took but four minutes, tide being dead high.

headline: Aiming for Greenwich, landing in Darien
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen sail across the Sound meaning to reach Greenwich but misjudge which side of Shippan Point to pass and end up at Darien. Roosevelt notes he has ridden his horse every day he has been home this season.

events.detail: Sails across the Sound with Emlen, missing Greenwich and fetching Darien
Has ridden his horse daily all summer

tr_quotes.text: My horse has done wonderfully this season; I have not missed riding him a single day when at home

headline: Doers of the word
summary: Roosevelt admires the scripture carved over his church door and writes that he puts no stock in faith without deeds. He has been reading the published memorial to his father and resolves to live as his father would have hoped.

events.detail: Reflects on the church motto about acting on faith
Reads the memorial volume to his late father

tr_quotes.text: I am no believer in faith without works.
With Gods help I shall try to lead such a life as Father would have wished me to.

headline: Woodcock in thick cover
summary: Roosevelt hunts woodcock over some 25 miles of rough country, where the birds now hide in dense brush. He misses more than half his shots and comes home with seven, he and the dog both worn out by the heat.

events.detail: Tramps about 25 miles after woodcock, killing seven

tr_quotes.text: I shot wretchedly; missing over half my birds.

headline: A birthday gift for Edith Carow
summary: For Edith Carow's 17th birthday, Roosevelt sends her a bonbonniere. His sister Corinne also writes Edith an affectionate letter about her future.

events.detail: Sends Edith Carow a bonbonniere for her birthday
Corinne writes warmly to Edith

tr_quotes.text: It being Edith C's 17th birthday, I sent her a bonbonierre

uncertain: Corinne's letter is listed but was not written by or to TR; not entered under letters.

headline: Jack Elliott comes to stay
summary: Roosevelt's good friend Jack Elliott arrives at Oyster Bay for a visit of five or six weeks.

events.detail: Jack Elliott arrives for an extended stay

tr_quotes.text: Dear old Jack Elliott arrived today, to stay five or six weeks.

headline: Sail, oar and paddle to Lloyd Neck
summary: With a following wind, Roosevelt and Jack Elliott make good time to Lloyd Neck using sail, oars and paddle together. They hunt the lagoons, lunch, fight their way out of the marsh at dead low tide and row home into a headwind, with two yellowlegs and two herons.

events.detail: Hunts the Lloyd Neck lagoons with Jack Elliott
Rows home against a headwind

headline: Six months gone, a glorious sail
summary: Roosevelt and Jack sail in a near-reefing breeze without shortening canvas. He calls Oyster Bay the ideal place for young men and wonders if anyone could be happier, while noting it has been six months since his father died.

events.detail: Sails with Jack Elliott in a stiff breeze
Marks six months since his father's death

tr_quotes.text: Oyster Bay is the perfection of a place for fellows; I often wonder if any one could have a happier time than I am having.
Six months ago
it seems so much longer.

headline: Harvard grades arrive
summary: Roosevelt's Harvard rank list comes, showing an average near 85, a ten-point gain over the year before, with his best marks in German and natural history. He is pleased and thinks his father would have been too, though he is laid up with cholera morbus.

events.detail: Receives his sophomore marks from Harvard, averaging about 85
Laid up with cholera morbus

tr_quotes.text: I am well satisfied; + and my dearest Father would have been so pleased.
Funnily enough I am rather laid up by an attack of cholera morbus.

headline: Missing church, thinking of Father
summary: Still ill, Roosevelt misses church for nearly the first time that year. With idle hours, a rarity for him, his thoughts keep returning to his father.

events.detail: Stays home from church while sick
Spends the idle day thinking of his father

tr_quotes.text: As usual when I have nothing to do (a rare event, thank fortune) I have been thinking a great deal of Father.

headline: Mosquito portage and a note from Edith
summary: Roosevelt and Jack row to Plum Point, haul the boat 200 yards over miserable, mosquito-thick ground into the big marsh behind Centre Island, then hunt, lunch and sail home. Edith Carow has sent a sweet thank-you for her birthday gift.

events.detail: Marsh expedition with Jack Elliott; one sand snipe
Receives a thank-you note from Edith Carow

headline: Riding the tide through Lloyd Neck marsh
summary: Roosevelt and Jack row to Lloyd Neck, going into the marsh as the tide rises and coming out as it falls. A stiff southerly holds them out until late afternoon. One yellowlegs, one sand snipe.

events.detail: Shoots through the Lloyd Neck marsh with Jack Elliott

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Nine hours after woodcock
summary: Roosevelt hunts woodcock from eight to five without stopping to eat or rest, testing new knickerbockers, gaiters and hunting shoes. The cover is so thick he misses two shots in three, yet he takes six birds and feels completely fresh.

events.detail: Nine-hour woodcock hunt, killing six birds

tr_quotes.text: I tried my new knickerbockers gaiters and hunting shoes, which worked to a charm.
had glorious sport, +, funnily enough, feel fresh as a lark.

headline: Edith visits; caught in a squall
summary: Edith Carow arrives for a two-week stay with Corinne. Roosevelt, Emlen and Jack sail to the Connecticut shore and run into a heavy rainstorm on the way back.

events.detail: Edith Carow arrives to visit Corinne for two weeks
Sails to Connecticut with Emlen and Jack Elliott

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Picnic sail and boxing lessons
summary: Roosevelt, Edith, Corinne, Jack and Emlen sail out for a picnic lunch at Yellowbanks. He starts teaching Jack to box, gets the better of Emlen in a bout, and loses to him at the rifle.

events.detail: Sailing picnic at Yellowbanks
Teaches Jack Elliott to spar and boxes Emlen
Emlen beats him at rifle shooting

headline: Rowing Edith; West's confession
summary: Roosevelt rows Edith out toward Lloyd Neck and spars with Jack and West. Riding with West, he hears all about his cousin's devotion to a young woman named Fanny and is touched by how smitten West is.

events.detail: Rows Edith out toward Lloyd Neck
Spars with Jack Elliott and West
West confides his love for Fanny on a ride

tr_quotes.text: It is really touching to see how much in love he is.

headline: Water lilies with Edith
summary: Roosevelt drives Edith to Cold Spring to gather water lilies, a lovely morning together. In the afternoon Elliott sails in on the Waterwitch with cousin Jack Roosevelt after a three-week cruise.

events.detail: Drives Edith to Cold Spring to pick water lilies
Elliott returns aboard the Waterwitch with Jack Roosevelt

tr_quotes.text: spending a lovely morning with her.

uncertain: 'Coldspring' taken as Cold Spring Harbor; 'Nell' is Elliott.

headline: Family sail and tea at West's
summary: Roosevelt, Elliott and Jack take their mother, Edith and Corinne sailing. That evening a large family party has tea at West's, after which Roosevelt and Edith walk up to the summer house. He worries his hard ride that day may have hurt his horse.

events.detail: Takes Mother, Edith and Corinne sailing with Elliott and Jack
Tea at West's with relatives and cousins
Goes up to the summer house with Edith

tr_quotes.text: My ride today was so long and hard that I am afraid it may have injured my horse.

uncertain: 'Jack' assumed to be Jack Elliott.

headline: Summer at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt is at Oyster Bay; no activities are recorded.

headline: Shooting a troublesome dog
summary: Having warned a dog's owner after the animal harassed him on horseback, Roosevelt carries out the threat while riding with West, killing it with his revolver as it runs beside his horse.

events.detail: Shoots a dog that had bothered him on rides

tr_quotes.text: rolling it over with my revolver very neatly as it ran alongside the horse.

headline: Sunday family prayers
summary: Roosevelt notes how much he values the family habit of morning and evening prayers on Sundays.

events.detail: Family prayers morning and evening

tr_quotes.text: I like our custom of having family prayers in the morning and evening of Sunday very much.

headline: A dawn gallop, then off on the Addie
summary: On a crisp, clear morning Roosevelt rides twenty miles at a gallop with Emlen. Around noon he, Emlen, West and Jack board the Addie for a short cruise, reaching New Haven about ten that night in light air.

events.detail: Twenty-mile gallop with Emlen
Sets out on a yachting cruise aboard the Addie
Reaches New Haven around 10 p.m.

headline: Lazy day under sail to New London
summary: Light winds keep the Addie under way until 8 p.m. before she reaches New London. The young men swim, read the New Symposium, climb the rigging and play whist.

events.detail: Sails from New Haven to New London
Reads the New Symposium aboard
Swimming, climbing the rigging and whist

tr_quotes.text: It is very lazy but very pleasant.

headline: Revolver practice off Greenport
summary: The party sails on to Greenport in fitful breezes. With hundreds of cartridges aboard, they fire their revolvers at anything that surfaces, from bottles and buoys to sharks and porpoises.

events.detail: Sails to Greenport
Revolver target practice from the yacht

tr_quotes.text: I never slept or ate better in my life.

headline: Along the Long Island shore
summary: In a steady breeze the Addie sails all day along Long Island's low, sandy shoreline. Roosevelt spends long stretches up in the crosstrees; the rest goes to whist and arguments about materialism and politics.

events.detail: Sails west along the Long Island coast
Whist and debates on materialism and politics

tr_quotes.text: I passed a good deal of time in the cross trees

headline: Cruise ends at Oyster Bay
summary: The Addie reaches Oyster Bay at 1 a.m. and the crew comes ashore for breakfast. Roosevelt has loved the cruise, and in the afternoon he goes sailing again with Jack and Alfred. Corinne writes Edith that her visit was worth another painful goodbye.

events.detail: Returns to Oyster Bay from the cruise
Afternoon sail with Jack Elliott and Alfred
Corinne writes to Edith Carow

tr_quotes.text: Have most heartily enjoyed the cruise,

uncertain: Corinne's letter to Edith is not TR's correspondence; noted as an event only.

headline: Hunting sea coots in vain
summary: Roosevelt and Jack row nearly twenty miles after sea coots without seeing a single one. George Minot arrives for a few days' visit.

events.detail: Rows almost 20 miles after sea coots, finding none
George Minot arrives to stay

headline: Uncertain about the future
summary: Roosevelt talks with Uncle Jim about what he will do with his life and admits he has no idea what follows college. Missing his father's guidance keenly, he decides his job for the next two years is plain: study hard and live as a brave Christian gentleman.

events.detail: Discusses his future at length with Uncle Jim
Grieves for his father's counsel

tr_quotes.text: I have absolutely no idea what I should do when I leave college.
my duty is clear - to study well and live like a brave Christian gentleman.

uncertain: 'Uncle Jim' taken as James King Gracie.

headline: Racing to Rye and back
summary: A strong westerly sends two boats across to Rye and back: Roosevelt and Alfred in the Meteor, with Elliott, Jack and George Minot crewing the Daphne. They lunch with the Bulkleys, where Roosevelt meets Miss Lee Berry.

events.detail: Sails the Meteor to Rye with Alfred
Lunch at the Bulkleys', meeting Miss Lee Berry

headline: Racing a squall to Rocky Point
summary: Roosevelt and Jack plan a night out in the skiff, but heavy rain sends them home. After lunch at Matinecock Point a fierce northwest squall hits off Oak Bluff, and they run before it under sail to Rocky Point, taking on a lot of water.

events.detail: Skiff trip with Jack Elliott, lunching at Matinecock Point
Caught in a heavy squall and runs for Rocky Point

tr_quotes.text: staunch though the little boat is, we shipped a good deal of water.

headline: Grim news about Hal Minot
summary: George Minot tells Roosevelt that his brother Hal, a close friend, has lost his reason and been placed in an asylum. Roosevelt grieves for the gentle, bright young man and his family. Later Uncle Hill and Aunt Susie come to stay.

events.detail: Learns his friend Hal Minot has been committed to an asylum
Uncle Hill and Aunt Susie arrive

tr_quotes.text: he is as sweet and gentle a fellow as I have ever seen, and very bright; and a true friend to me

uncertain: Two words in the diary are illegible in the record.

headline: Sad news, then dinner at the Union League
summary: Overnighting in New York, Roosevelt visits Cassin, who is slowly dying, and learns that Cousin Sam Roosevelt has died. Still low about Hal Minot, he dines that evening at the Union League Club with Jack Roosevelt and Emlen.

events.detail: Goes into New York for the night
Visits his dying friend Cassin
Learns of Cousin Sam Roosevelt's death
Dines at the Union League Club with Jack Roosevelt and Emlen

tr_quotes.text: Called on poor Cassin; he is dying by inches.

headline: Northbound for the Maine woods
summary: Roosevelt, West and Emlen board an early-morning train to Boston, bound for three weeks in the Maine woods. Writing of Hal Minot, he says his father's death has dulled his ability to grieve.

events.detail: Takes the morning train to Boston with West and Emlen

tr_quotes.text: Father's death has taken away much of my capacity for grieving.

headline: Arriving at Island Falls
summary: After an overnight train to Mattawamkeag, the party rides a buckboard to Island Falls, arriving at 8 p.m. Roosevelt is suffering a bad bout of asthma and misses his horse.

events.detail: Overnight train to Mattawamkeag, then buckboard to Island Falls
Has a bad attack of asthma

tr_quotes.text: Have a pretty bad attack of asthma

uncertain: The record has 'Highland Island Falls'; it is read as Island Falls.

headline: Psalm 19 and a Methodist meeting
summary: Roosevelt walks, reads his Bible and memorizes Psalm 19. With no church in Island Falls, he attends a Methodist meeting in the schoolhouse. Thoughts of Hal Minot bring back his grief for his father.

events.detail: Learns Psalm 19 by heart
Attends a Methodist meeting in the schoolhouse

tr_quotes.text: I try whenever I can only to recall his grand and beautful life. Oh Father, Father!

headline: Partridge hunt, seven months on
summary: Seven months after his father's death, Roosevelt spends the whole day after partridges without seeing one.

events.detail: Hunts partridges all day without sighting any

tr_quotes.text: Spent the day hunting partridges but did not even see one.

headline: Paddling down to Mattawamkeag Lake
summary: The party heads downstream to camp at the foot of Mattawamkeag Lake, the others in a bateau with guide Sewall while Roosevelt goes ahead by canoe with guide Dow. He enjoys the paddling and woods walking but misses every shot at pigeons and ducks.

events.detail: Canoes downstream to Mattawamkeag Lake with guide Dow
Several misses at pigeons and ducks
Sets up camp at the foot of the lake

tr_quotes.text: I had good fun paddling, and tramping through the woods

uncertain: 'Will T.' identified as Will Thompson from the 9/23 'Thornson'; guides taken as Bill Sewall and Wilmot Dow.

headline: A loon at long range and a quiet ramble
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen canoe the lake; Roosevelt fires at a loon over a hundred yards away and nearly hits it. In the afternoon they hike about ten miles after partridge, taking one ruffed grouse, and he praises Emlen as a loyal companion.

events.detail: Rifle shots at a distant loon from the canoe
Ten-mile woods walk after partridge; one ruffed grouse

tr_quotes.text: he and I are great companions and he is a true friend.

headline: Rainy day in camp
summary: Rain keeps the party under canvas with books, cards and gun cleaning, eating duck, partridge, trout and pickerel. Roosevelt and Emlen sit three hours in the wet waiting for ducks and come back empty-handed.

events.detail: Rainy day in camp with cards and gun cleaning
Waits in a blind for ducks with Emlen; no luck

headline: Still raining at camp
summary: Another wet day of reading, euchre, whist and rifle practice in camp. Roosevelt waits for ducks again with one long miss, and kills a bat and a nighthawk.

events.detail: Stays in camp, playing cards and shooting at targets
Kills a bat and a nighthawk

tr_quotes.text: I killed a bat and a nighthawk.

headline: Missing foxes across the river
summary: When the rain stops at noon, Roosevelt hikes fifteen miles with Sewall and comes back with nothing. He misses two foxes at about sixty yards and is fed up with his week of poor shooting.

events.detail: Fifteen-mile hunt with Sewall; misses two foxes

tr_quotes.text: I am disgusted with myself.

headline: Bible, guns and specimens
summary: Roosevelt reads his Bible in the morning, then fills the afternoon cleaning guns and labeling specimens before a swim in the mill race.

events.detail: Morning Bible reading
Labels specimens
Bathes in the mill race

tr_quotes.text: Read my bible in the morning

headline: Thirty miles along the Mattawamkeag
summary: After a frosty night, Roosevelt and Sewall hike thirty miles near the Mattawamkeag River, on the move from eight to seven save a half-hour lunch. He gets only four shots, bagging a rabbit, a merganser and two grouse, but loves the walk.

events.detail: Thirty-mile hunting tramp with Sewall

tr_quotes.text: But enjoyed the walk greatly.

headline: A night in a wigwam
summary: Roosevelt, West and guide Dow paddle to the head of the lake and hunt the sloughs and bogs with middling luck, taking two ducks. The three camp overnight in a wigwam on a meager supper.

events.detail: Hunts the bogs at the head of the lake by canoe
Camps out in a wigwam

headline: Up at four for ducks
summary: Up before dawn, the three hunt ducks and see none. Back at the main camp, Roosevelt walks about ten miles with Will Dow for four shots, a merganser and three grouse, and decides moccasins are the best footwear for the woods.

events.detail: Pre-dawn duck hunt, unsuccessful
Ten-mile hunt with Will Dow

tr_quotes.text: I like moccasins to walk through the woods with very much.

headline: Through alder and cedar swamps
summary: Roosevelt hikes about fifteen miles, three of them through some of the hardest swamp walking he has known. He takes a spruce partridge among the cedars and a ruffed grouse up on a hemlock ridge.

events.detail: Fifteen-mile hike through swamps, shooting partridges
Takes a spruce grouse and a ruffed grouse

headline: Fooled by a decoy duck
summary: On a ten-mile walk with Sewall, Roosevelt stalks and kills a duck on a small lake. The others then trick him with a dead duck propped up to look alive in a pond. He has bathed in the mill race daily.

events.detail: Stalks and shoots a duck with Sewall
Falls for a prank with a propped-up dead duck

tr_quotes.text: Was nicely sold by the boys with a dead duck placed in a life like attitude in a pond.

headline: Autumn color in the Maine woods
summary: Roosevelt and Emlen hunt in the afternoon; Emlen never fires, and Roosevelt misses a duck but drops a partridge. The leaves are turning, and he counts the trip a real success.

events.detail: Afternoon hunt with Emlen; one ruffed grouse

tr_quotes.text: The leaves are now beginning to turn and the woods are perfectly beautiful.

headline: Quiet Sunday in camp
summary: Roosevelt passes Sunday much as he did the week before.

events.detail: A quiet Sunday in camp

tr_quotes.text: Spent the day much as last Sunday.

headline: Breaking camp by bateau
summary: The party breaks camp and heads back to Island Falls in the clumsy bateau: Sewall paddling, Roosevelt and Dow at the oars, Thompson trolling, and West and Emlen in the bow watching for game. Roosevelt spends the afternoon in the woods with West.

events.detail: Returns to Island Falls by bateau
Afternoon woods walk with West; one ruffed grouse

uncertain: 'Thornson' read as Thompson.

headline: Twenty-five miles with Dow
summary: Roosevelt hikes 25 miles with Dow, taking a woodcock and two partridges. Game has been scarce all trip, but he has loved it, and the party has not had one quarrel.

events.detail: Twenty-five-mile hunt with Dow

tr_quotes.text: There has been absolutely no disagreement between any members of the party.

uncertain: 'log cock' likely a woodcock.

headline: Hunting from a buckboard
summary: Roosevelt rides around all day in a buckboard, Will Dow at his side, climbing down each time they spot a partridge. He gets five grouse and sees a fox.

events.detail: Drives the roads with Dow, stopping for partridges; five grouse
Sees a fox

headline: Leaving Maine
summary: The party drives by wagon to Mattawamkeag and boards the night train for Boston. His companions will continue to New York; Roosevelt is bound back to Harvard.

events.detail: Wagon to Mattawamkeag and night train for Boston

headline: Back at Harvard, a surprise invitation
summary: Roosevelt returns to Cambridge for his junior year to a warm welcome. To his astonishment the Porcellian Club asks him to join, and he feels he must decline because he belongs to the A.D. Club, though he wishes otherwise. His sister Corinne turns 17.

events.detail: Returns to Harvard for his junior year
Offered membership in the Porcellian Club
Corinne's 17th birthday

tr_quotes.text: To my great surprise I was offered the Porcellian; of course I could not accept, being a member of the A.D. - but I wish I could.

headline: Settling into the junior-year routine
summary: Roosevelt finds his classes and lab work will fill about twenty hours a week, with an 8 a.m. recitation daily, Saturdays included. Harry Shaw and Dick Saltonstall each invite him for Sunday, and his club table at Mrs. Wilson's serves excellent meals.

events.detail: Sizes up a schedule of about 20 class hours a week
Invitations from Harry Shaw and Dick Saltonstall

headline: Sunday church in Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt goes to church and plans to resume teaching Sunday school in a week or two.

events.detail: Attends church

tr_quotes.text: I shall not take up my sunday school till next Sunday or the one after.

headline: Down to work and the rifle club
summary: Roosevelt starts studying in earnest and joins the rifle club, meaning to shoot regularly this year. In New York the cables for the Brooklyn Bridge are finished.

events.detail: Begins his regular course of study
Joins the Harvard rifle club
Cable-spinning on the Brooklyn Bridge is completed

tr_quotes.text: I joined the rifle club; I am going to practice pretty regularly with the rifle this year.

headline: Into the Glee Club
summary: Roosevelt is voted into the Harvard Glee Club.

events.detail: Elected to the Glee Club

tr_quotes.text: Was elected into the Glee club.

headline: At the D.K.E., but not drinking
summary: Roosevelt attends the first D.K.E. meeting of the year. He finds its drinking tiresome as a steady diet, though fun now and then; he does not drink there, drinks very little anyway, and will not smoke before he is 21.

events.detail: Attends the first D.K.E. meeting of the year

tr_quotes.text: I shall not begin smoking till I am twenty one; as it is, I drink very little.

headline: First meeting of the Art Club
summary: Roosevelt goes to the opening meeting of the Art Club and enjoys it.

events.detail: Attends the Art Club's first meeting

tr_quotes.text: Attended the first meeting of the Art Club, and found it very pleasant.

headline: Favorite courses: philosophy and economics
summary: Roosevelt ranks his courses: philosophy and political economy come first, natural history is engaging if less so than last year, and the rest interest him little.

events.detail: Reflects on which of his courses he likes best

tr_quotes.text: Of my studies this year I like best the philosophy and political economy

headline: Morning at the rifle range
summary: Roosevelt spends the morning shooting at the range.

events.detail: Morning of rifle practice

tr_quotes.text: Spent the morning at the rifle range.

headline: Communion Sunday at Cambridge
summary: Roosevelt marks Communion Sunday.

events.detail: Observes Communion Sunday

tr_quotes.text: Communion Sunday

headline: Hard work, with holidays ahead
summary: Roosevelt is studying hard, but his strong average last year earns him optional recitations, so he expects some three weeks of winter holidays.

events.detail: Works hard; optional recitations promise winter time off

tr_quotes.text: I am working pretty hard now

headline: Boxing lessons resume
summary: Roosevelt starts up again with his boxing teacher and writes his mother an affectionate letter saying his studies take six or seven hours a day.

events.detail: Resumes lessons with his boxing teacher
Writes to his mother about his studies

letters.topic: Affectionate note reporting six or seven hours of study daily

tr_quotes.text: Darling, beloved, little motherling

headline: Caught between two clubs
summary: After two drunk club men argue about him and reveal his preference for the Porcellian, the A.D. members vote to let Roosevelt choose between the clubs, since he never formally joined theirs. Knowing either choice will hurt someone, he spends a miserable day weighing what honor requires.

events.detail: The A.D. Club offers to release him to choose the Porcellian

tr_quotes.text: it is terribly hard to know what is the honorable thing to do.

headline: At Harvard
summary: Roosevelt is at Cambridge; no activities are recorded.

headline: Choosing the Porcellian
summary: Roosevelt settles it and joins the Porcellian, listing classmates on each side: Weld, Shaw, Trimble, Morgan and Griswold among the Porcellian men; Bob Bacon, Billy Hooper and others in the A.D.

events.detail: Decides to join the Porcellian Club

tr_quotes.text: Have finally decided to go into the Porcellian

uncertain: 'Bob Bacon' rendered as Robert Bacon, TR's classmate.

headline: Notes on classmates
summary: Roosevelt records that Arthur Hooper has left Harvard and that Brooks and Peters have been dropped. He has warmed to Charley Ware and Harry Shaw, and calls Harry Chapin a perfect trump.

events.detail: Notes departures and friendships among classmates

tr_quotes.text: Charley Ware is a capital fellow and a thoroughly good one too

headline: Charley Dickey under the same roof
summary: Roosevelt is glad to have Charley Dickey living in his house and feels he has helped him. He writes Bamie that more than half his college career is behind him.

events.detail: Enjoys having Charley Dickey in his lodging house
Writes to his sister Bamie

letters.topic: Notes he has passed the midpoint of his Harvard years

tr_quotes.text: It makes it very homelike to have old Charley Dickey in the same house with me.
Over half my college career is done.

headline: Lab work eats the hours
summary: One of Roosevelt's natural history courses demands heavy laboratory work, which he enjoys though it devours his time.

events.detail: Heavy lab work for a natural history course

headline: Sparring and gratitude to the A.D.
summary: Roosevelt has been boxing with several classmates and writes that the A.D. men have handled the club episode very decently.

events.detail: Spars with classmates

tr_quotes.text: The A.D. men have behaved like trumps.

headline: Who sits at his table
summary: Roosevelt lists his dining-table companions: Weld, Chapin, Ware, Washburn, Ellis, Peters and Saltonstall.

events.detail: Notes the members of his club dining table

headline: Dinner with the Hoopers
summary: Roosevelt enjoys dinner at the Hoopers' and is pleased to meet Miss Jeannie once more.

events.detail: Dines with the Hooper family

uncertain: Miss Jeannie's surname assumed to be Hooper.

headline: Off to Chestnut Hill with Dick Saltonstall
summary: After boxing Tucker Burr to a standstill, Roosevelt rides in Dick Saltonstall's buggy to the Saltonstall home at Chestnut Hill, where the family's kindness makes him feel completely at home.

events.detail: Spars with Tucker Burr
Driven by buggy to the Saltonstall home at Chestnut Hill

tr_quotes.text: All his family are just too sweet to me for anything, and the whole house is so homelike.

headline: Meeting Alice Lee
summary: Roosevelt rambles through the woods alongside Dick, Dick's sister Rose and their cousin Alice Lee, whom he finds sweet and pretty. The group dines and takes tea at the Whitneys', dancing and singing until they drive home around eleven. He would marry Alice in 1880.

events.detail: Woods walk with Dick and Rose Saltonstall and Alice Lee
Dinner, tea and dancing at the Whitneys'

tr_quotes.text: a very sweet pretty girl.

headline: Chestnutting with Alice Lee
summary: After church, Roosevelt spends the afternoon gathering chestnuts with Alice Lee.

events.detail: Morning church
Gathers chestnuts with Alice Lee

headline: Back to Cambridge and the Glee Club
summary: Roosevelt returns by carriage to Cambridge early in the day and that evening hears some lovely singing at the Glee Club.

events.detail: Returns from Chestnut Hill to Cambridge
Evening at the Glee Club

headline: Town and gown scuffle
summary: A political meeting for Benjamin Butler and Denis Kearney sets off a brawl between students and townspeople, and Roosevelt enjoys watching the crew pile in.

events.detail: Witnesses a town-and-gown fight at a political rally

tr_quotes.text: It was good fun to see the crew wade in.

headline: Arguing with Mill, tiring of Ferrier
summary: Roosevelt finds political economy absorbing even though he does not fully accept John Stuart Mill, and is losing patience with Ferrier's philosophy.

events.detail: Studies Mill's political economy and Ferrier's philosophy

tr_quotes.text: I am very much interested in the Political Economy, although I by no means altogether agree with Mill.

headline: A long walk and a family scandal
summary: Roosevelt hikes with Jack Tebbetts, who has grown on him. Then a letter brings word that his cousin Cornelius has married a French actress, which Roosevelt condemns harshly in his diary.

events.detail: Long walk with Jack Tebbetts
Hears that cousin Cornelius has married a French actress

tr_quotes.text: He is a disgrace to the family - the vulgar brute.

uncertain: Which Cornelius is meant is not specified beyond 'T.R.'s cousin'.

headline: Evening boat to New York
summary: Roosevelt takes the night boat to New York for a break, admitting he has not studied as hard as he should in some subjects and vowing to buckle down on his return.

events.detail: Night steamer from Boston area to New York

tr_quotes.text: as soon as I come home from this holiday I shall set to with a will.

headline: Home with family at Oyster Bay
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with West, who is upset over Cornelius's marriage, visits Aunt Annie, lunches with West and Alfred, and reaches Oyster Bay in the afternoon, happy to be with his family. All look well except Elliott.

events.detail: Breakfast and lunch with West and Alfred
Morning with Aunt Annie Gracie
Goes out to Oyster Bay

tr_quotes.text: It is just lovely to be back with the family again.

uncertain: 'Doc' appears to be West; 'Nell' is Elliott.

headline: Turning twenty
summary: Roosevelt marks his 20th birthday at Oyster Bay with his mother and sisters, but the day is shadowed by longing for his father. He also shoots two gray squirrels.

events.detail: Spends his 20th birthday with his mother and sisters
Shoots two gray squirrels

tr_quotes.text: Oh, Father, sometimes I feel as though I would give half my life to see you but for a moment!

uncertain: 'Muffie, Bysie and Pussie' read as his mother, Bamie and Corinne.

headline: Rough water around Centre Island
summary: In a stiff north wind Roosevelt rows around Centre Island through seas that half-fill his boat, then sails home fast from Pine Island. An afternoon walk with his gun turns up nothing.

events.detail: Rows around Centre Island in heavy seas
Sails home from Pine Island
Afternoon woods walk with gun; no game

tr_quotes.text: I sailed home from Pine Island at a tremendous speed.

headline: Coots and a checker-back loon
summary: Sailing for ducks in light, shifting wind, Roosevelt finds few birds but plenty of fun: he drops two coots from a flock, runs down a loon after a lengthy pursuit, and misses an old squaw.

events.detail: Duck hunting under sail; two surf ducks and a loon

tr_quotes.text: The wind was light and baffling and we saw but few birds but had capital fun.

headline: Drenched and empty-handed
summary: A southeaster with steady rain squalls soaks Roosevelt on a duck-hunting sail, and he comes home with nothing after missing a grebe.

events.detail: Sails for ducks in a southeaster; no birds

tr_quotes.text: I missed a good shot at a grebe.

headline: Bad luck with the weather
summary: Rain again. Roosevelt grumbles that his whole break has been spoiled by weather: too rough one day, too calm the next, then two days of rain.

events.detail: Rain keeps him in at Oyster Bay

tr_quotes.text: Rainy again! I have had most awful luck in weather this time.

uncertain: The record adds its compiler's family tree of the Saltonstall and Lee families of Chestnut Hill; those names are listed as subjects only.
